Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 25, verse 4–6:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved say﴾ meaning: the polytheists of Quraysh. Muqatil said: it is the saying of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith from the Banu Abd al-Dar. ﴿This is not﴾ i.e., "what is this," meaning the Qur'an. ﴿except a fabrication﴾ i.e., a lie. ﴿which he has invented﴾ i.e., he fabricated it from his own self. ﴿And others have helped him therein﴾. Mujahid said: they mean the Jews. Muqatil said: they pointed to ʿAddas, the freedman of Huwaytib, and Yasar, the slave of Amir ibn al-Hadrami, and Jabr, also a freedman of Amir, and all three were from the People of the Book.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So they have produced an injustice and a falsehood﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "they have come with an injustice and a falsehood," and when the preposition (bāʾ) was dropped, the verb reached its object and took the accusative. Al-Zur (zūr) means lying. ﴿And they say, "Legends of the former peoples"﴾. The meaning: and they say, "What he has brought is the legends of the former peoples." We have explained this in (al-Anʿam: 25). The exegetes said: the one who said this was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith.

The meaning of ﴿iktataba-hā﴾ is that he ordered it to be written down for him. Ibn Masʿud, Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi and Talha ibn Musarrif read "uktutibahā" with the first tā' raised and the second kasra'd, and the beginning (of the word) on their reading is with a raised hamza. ﴿So it is dictated to him﴾ i.e., it is read to him so that he may memorize it, not so that he may write it, because he was not a scribe. ﴿in the morning and in the evening﴾ i.e., at dawn and in the afternoon. ﴿Say﴾ to them, O Muhammad: ﴿He who knows the secret﴾ meaning: the Qur'an, ﴿[is the One] who sent it down, He who knows the secret [and open] in the heavens and the earth﴾ i.e., nothing is hidden from Him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 25, verse 7–9:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they say﴾ meaning the polytheists, ﴿"What is this Messenger that he eats food"﴾. They denied that the Messenger could be a human being who eats food and walks in the markets as other people walk, seeking livelihood. The meaning is: he is neither an angel nor a king, for angels do not eat, and kings do not debase themselves in the markets. So they were astonished that he should be equal to humans, not distinguished from them (p-74) in anything. Yet God made him a human so that he would be of the same kind as those to whom he was sent, and He did not make him a king who refrains from walking in the markets, for that is the conduct of tyrants, and because he was commanded to call them, so he needed to walk among them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿"Why has an angel not been sent down to him"﴾. This is because they said to him: Ask your Lord to send an angel with you to confirm you, and to give you gardens, palaces and treasures. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿"Or a treasure be thrown down to him"﴾, that is, a treasure be sent down to him from the sky, ﴿"or he have a garden from which he may eat"﴾, that is, an orchard from whose fruits he may eat. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read: "yakulu minha" (ياكل منها) with the ya', meaning the Prophet ﷺ. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "na'kulu" (نأكل) with the nun. Abu 'Ali said: the meaning is that he would have a superiority over us in virtue by our eating from his garden. The rest of the verse is explained in (Bani Isra'il: 47).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿"Look"﴾ O Muhammad, ﴿"how they have struck for you comparisons"﴾ when they described you as bewitched, as a soothsayer, a madman and a poet, ﴿"so they have strayed"﴾ by this from guidance, ﴿"and they cannot find a way"﴾. Regarding this there are two statements.

One: they cannot find a way out of the comparisons they have struck. This was said by Mujahid, and the meaning is that they lied and did not find for their claim any proof or evidence. al-Farra' said: they cannot find any stratagem regarding your affair.

The second: they cannot find a way to obedience. This was said by al-Suddi.

Ibn ʿAmir read *nahshuruhum* and *fa-naqulu* with *nun* in both places. The subject is the polytheists. ﴿And what they worship﴾: Mujahid said, it means ʿIsa, ʿUzayr, and the angels. ʿIkrima and al-Dahhak said, it means the idols, and God gives the idols permission to speak and addresses them. ﴿So He will say: "Did you lead My servants astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾, meaning: did you order them to worship you? ﴿They will say﴾, meaning the idols: ﴿Glory be to You﴾, they declare God far above having any other worshipped besides Him. ﴿It was not for us to take any allies besides You﴾, meaning, to take as protectors. The meaning is: it was not fitting for us to worship anyone other than You, so how could we call people to worship us? This answer shows that they did not order them to worship them. Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman al-Sulami, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Qatada, Abu Ja'far, Ibn Ya'mur, and ʿAsim al-Jahdari read *an nuttakhadha* with a *damma* on the *nun* and a *fatha* on the *kha'*, meaning a passive form. Then they mentioned the cause of their disbelief, saying: ﴿But You gave them enjoyment﴾, meaning You lengthened their lives and widened their provision, ﴿until they forgot the Reminder﴾, meaning they abandoned belief in the Qur'an and taking warning from it, ﴿and they were a people lost﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: *bur* means "ruined." In another narration he said: in the dialect of the Azd of ʿUman, *bur* means "corrupt." Ibn Qutayba said: it derives from *bara yabur*, when something perishes and becomes void. One says *bara al-ta'am* when food becomes unsalable, and *baratil-ayyim* when a woman is no longer desired. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to seek refuge from *bawar al-ayyim*. He said: Abu ʿUbayda said: one says *rajul bur* and *qawm bur*, which are not pluralized or dualized. He cited the verse of the poet:

"O Messenger of the Sovereign, my tongue is a mender:
I have not torn anything while I am *bur*."

We have also heard *rajul ba'ir*, and we have seen that they sometimes pluralize the pattern *fa'il* as *fu'l*, such as *ta'idh* and *'uudh*, and *sharif* and *shurf*. The exegetes said: then it will be said to the disbelievers: ﴿So they have denied you﴾, meaning the worshipped ones have denied you in your claim that they are gods. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Mu'adh al-Qari', and Ibn Shanbudh, on the authority of Qunbul, read *bima yaqulun* with *ya*. The meaning: they denied you by their saying: ﴿Glory be to You, it was not for us﴾, and so on. This is the view of most scholars. Ibn Zayd said: the address is to the believers. The meaning: the polytheists denied you by what you say, that Muhammad is the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

His saying, Exalted is He: (So they cannot avert [punishment] nor [obtain] help). Most readers read it with *ya*, and in it there are two possibilities.

One: the worshipped ones cannot avert the punishment from you, nor give you help.

The second: the disbelievers cannot avert God's punishment from themselves, nor help themselves.

Hafs, on the authority of ʿAsim, read *tastatiʿun* with *ta'*, and the address is to the disbelievers. Ibn Qutayba related from Yunus al-Basri that he said: *al-sarf* is "stratagem," from their saying: "he is *yatasarraf*" (he manages affairs cleverly).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever of you wrongs﴾, meaning by associating partners with God, ﴿We will make him taste﴾ in the Hereafter. ʿAsim al-Jahdari, al-Dahhak, and Abu al-Jawza' [and Qatada] read *yadhuqhu* with *ya*. ﴿A great punishment﴾, meaning severe. ﴿And We did not send before you any messengers except that they [too] ate food and walked in the markets.﴾ al-Zajjaj said: there is an omitted element in the verse. If it is asked: why is *innahum* here read with a *kasra*, while in [Surat Bara'a, 9:54] in His saying: ﴿that their expenditures will not be accepted from them except that they [innahum] ...﴾ it is with a *fatha*? He meant: "[one] whose tears..."

Muqatil said: "the sky" means the heavens, which are split open from white clouds resembling mist, and the angels descend at their splitting.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 25, verse 32–34:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ That is, just as the Torah, the Gospel and the Psalms were sent down. Then Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning: We sent it down in this manner, in installments, because the meaning of what they said was: Why was it sent down to him in installments? So it was said: We sent it down in this way ﴿so that We may strengthen your heart thereby﴾, meaning: so that We may fortify your heart with it, and you may increase in insight. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they do not bring you any example﴾, meaning the polytheists, ﴿[to argue] with which they strike at you in disputation and in nullifying your affair﴾, ﴿but We bring you the truth﴾, meaning: that which is the truth, so that you may repel their plotting with it, ﴿and a better explanation﴾ than their example; and tafsir (explanation) means clarification and disclosure.

Muqatil said: Then He informed of their dwelling place in the Hereafter, saying: ﴿Those who will be gathered on their faces (p-89) to Hell﴾. That is because the disbelievers of Mecca said: Muhammad and his companions are the worst of Allah's creation, so this verse was revealed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those are worse in place﴾, meaning: in station and destination, ﴿and further astray in way﴾, meaning: in religion and path, than the believers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 25, verse 45–52:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Have you not considered your Lord?﴾ That is: consider the action of your Lord. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "Have you not known?" so it is from seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb, i.e., knowledge). It may also be from seeing with the eye, so the meaning is: "Have you not seen how your Lord extended the shadow?" The shadow is from the time of the break of dawn until the time of sunrise. ﴿And had He willed, He would have made it still﴾ That is: fixed and constant, not moving. ﴿Then We made the sun over it an indicator﴾ The sun is an indicator of the shadow; were it not for the sun, the shadow would not be recognized as something, just as were it not for the light, darkness would not be recognized. Thus all things are known by their opposites.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then We draw it in toward Us, a gradual withdrawal﴾ meaning: the shadow. ﴿A gradual withdrawal﴾ and regarding it there are two statements.

One: swiftly. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: secretly (khafiyyan). This was said by Mujahid.

Regarding the time of the shadow's withdrawal there are two statements. One: at sunrise the shadow is withdrawn, and its spread-out parts are gathered by the sun's shining upon it until it is abrogated (tansakhuhu) bit by bit. The second: at sunset the parts of the shadow are withdrawn after the sun sets, and each part of it is replaced by a part of the darkness.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it is He who made for you the night as a garment﴾ That is: a covering with its darkness, because its darkness covers persons and envelops them in the manner that a garment envelops its wearer. ﴿And sleep as rest (subatan)﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, rest (rahah). From this comes the name of Saturday (yawm al-sabt), because creation was gathered on Friday, and the completion of it was on Saturday; so it was said to the Children of Israel: "Rest on this day and do nothing in it," so it was named Yawm al-Sabt, that is, the Day of Rest. The root of sabt is stretching out, and whoever stretches out rests. Ibn al-Anbari said: the root of sabt is cutting; so the meaning is: "We made sleep a cutting off of your works."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He made the day a resurrection (nushuran)﴾ regarding it there are two statements. One: you disperse in it seeking provision, said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the spirit is revived by wakefulness just as it is revived by resurrection; related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds﴾ We have explained it in (al-A'raf: 75) up to His saying: ﴿And We send down from the sky pure water (ma'an tahuran)﴾ meaning: rain. Al-Azhari said: tahur in the language means pure and purifying. And tahur is what one purifies oneself with, like the wudu' water with which one performs ablution, and the fatur with which one breaks the fast.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That We may give life thereby to a dead land﴾ Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza' and Abu Ja'far read: "maytan" with shaddah. Al-Zajjaj said: the word baldah is feminine, but it was said "maytan" because the meaning of baldah and balad is the same. Others said: he said "maytan" because by baldah he intended the place. The meaning of describing the land as dead has already been mentioned [al-A'raf: 57]; and the meaning of ﴿and to give drink﴾ [al-Furqan: 49]???. Abu Mijlaz, Abu Raja', al-Dahhak, al-A'mash and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "wa-nusqiyahu" with a fatha on the nun. As for "anasiyy", al-Zajjaj said: it is the plural of insiyy, like kursiyy and karasiyy; it may also be the plural of insan, with the ya' replacing the nun; the original is anasin, like sarahin. Abu Mijlaz, (p-95) al-Dahhak, Abu al-'Aliyah and 'Asim al-Jahdari read: "wa-anasiyya" with the ya' lightened.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly distributed it among them﴾ meaning the rain: among them once for this town, and once for that. ﴿That they may remember﴾ That is: that they may reflect upon the blessings of Allah upon them, so that they praise Him. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "liyadhkuru" with a light dhal. Abu 'Ali said: yadhkuru carries the meaning of yatadhakkaru. ﴿But most of the people refuse except ingratitude﴾ and they are those who say, "We were given rain by such-and-such a star (nawʾ)," and so they disbelieved in the blessing of Allah. ﴿And if We willed, We would have sent into every town a warner﴾ The meaning: We sent you to all the towns, out of the greatness of your honour. ﴿So do not obey the disbelievers﴾ and that is because the disbelievers of Makkah called him to the religion of their fathers. ﴿And strive against them with it﴾ that is, with the Qur'an, ﴿a great striving﴾ that is: complete and intense.

The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 25, verses 53–55:

Allah's words: ﴿And it is He who released the two seas⦈. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, He let them flow freely alongside each other. You say *marastu al-dabbata* and *amrastuha* ("I let the animal loose") when you let it graze. From this is the hadith, "*Marijat* (p-96) their covenants and their trusts," meaning they became mixed up. The commentators (*mufassirun*, those who write tafsir, or Qur'anic exegesis) said: The meaning is that He sent them along their courses so that they do not meet, and salt does not mix with sweet water, nor sweet water with salt. His words ﴿This﴾, meaning one of the two seas, ﴿is sweet﴾, that is, pleasant. It is said: *adhuba al-ma'u yadh'ubu 'udhuba*, so it is *'adhb* (sweet). Al-Zajjaj said: *Al-furat* is an adjective of *al-'adhb*, and it is the sweetest of waters. *Al-ujaj* is an adjective of the salt water, and it is the bitter, extremely bitter. Ibn Qutayba said: It is the saltiest water. It was also said: It is the water mixed with bitterness. It is said *ma' milh* (salt water) and not *malih*. *Al-barzakh* means the barrier. Regarding this barrier there are two views.

The first: It is a barrier from the power of Allah, the Exalted. This is what most of them said. Al-Zajjaj said: To the eye they appear mixed, but in the power of Allah they are separate, and neither mixes with the other. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: I saw near 'Abbadan in the Basra marshlands the sweet water flowing down the Tigris toward the sea, and the tide coming in from the sea, and they meet, yet neither water mixes with the other. The sea water appears a deep green, and the Tigris water a light red. Then the one who draws water comes and fills his bucket with Tigris water, sweet and unmixed with anything, while beside him, in the same place, is sea water.

The second: The barrier is the land and the dry ground. This is the view of al-Hasan. The first view is more correct.

Allah's words: ﴿and a forbidding barrier﴾. Al-Farra' said: That is, a forbidden, prohibited thing, that one of them should overcome the other.

(p-97) Allah's words: ﴿And it is He who created man from water﴾, that is, from a drop (*nutfa*), a human being. ﴿Then He made him one with lineage and marriage﴾, that is, one possessing lineage and in-law ties. 'Ali, peace be upon him, said: Lineage is that whose marriage is unlawful, and in-law ties are that whose marriage is lawful. Al-Dahhak said: Lineage is seven, which is His words, ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ up to His words ﴿and the daughters of the sister﴾, and in-law ties are five, which is His words, ﴿And your mothers who have nursed you﴾ up to His words ﴿from your loins﴾ [An-Nisa' 23]. Tawus said: Fosterage is part of in-law ties. Ibn Qutayba said: ﴿Lineage﴾ means kinship by blood, and ﴿in-law ties﴾ means kinship by marriage. Everything that comes from the husband's side, like the father and brother, are *al-ahmaa'* (the husband's relatives), singular *hama*, like *qafa*; and *hamu*, like *abu*; and *hamʼ* (hamzated, with a sukun on the mim), and *ham*, like *ab*. The mother-in-law of a woman is *hama*, and there is no other form for it apart from this. Everything from the wife's side are *al-akhtan* (the wife's relatives). And *al-sihr* (in-law ties) includes all of that. Ibn Faris related from al-Khalil that he said: For the people of a man's household only *akhtan* is used, and for the people of a woman's household only *asbar* is used. Some Arabs make them all *asbar*. *Al-sihr* also means melting something. Al-Mawardi mentioned that marriages were called *sihr* because people mix through them, just as a substance mixes when it is melted.

Allah's words: ﴿And the disbeliever is ever a helper against his Lord﴾. On this there are four views.

The first: He is a helper of Satan against his Lord, because his worship of idols is aid to Satan.

The second: He is a helper of the polytheists in preventing them from affirming the oneness of Allah, the Exalted.

The third: He is a helper against the allies of his Lord.

The fourth: ﴿the disbeliever was against his Lord, insignificant and humiliated﴾, from your saying *zahartu bi-fulan* when you put someone behind your back and paid him no attention. They said: The disbeliever here is meant to be Abu Jahl.

**Section**

The scholars of naskh (abrogation) have two views concerning this verse.

The first is that it is abrogated (mansukh). There are three views on what abrogates it. The first is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever kills a believer intentionally, his recompense is Hell﴾ [An-Nisa: 93]; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, who used to say, "This [verse] is Meccan, and the one in An-Nisa is Medinan." The second is that it was abrogated by His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive association with Him, but He forgives what is less than that﴾ (An-Nisa: 48). The third is that the first was abrogated by the second, which is His saying ﴿except for those who repent﴾.

The second view is that it is muhkam (not abrogated), and that the eternal abiding was due only to the combination of polytheism with killing and fornication. The weakness of the first view is evident, because killing does not necessitate eternal abiding according to the majority; we have explained this in Surah An-Nisa: 93. Polytheism is not forgiven if the polytheist dies upon it, and an exception (istithna') is not an abrogation.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except those who repent﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "We recited during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for two years: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾. Then ﴿except those who repent﴾ was revealed. I never saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejoice at anything as he rejoiced at it, and at ﴿Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory﴾ [Al-Fath: 1]."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾. They differed concerning the manner of this replacement and the time at which it occurs. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah will replace their polytheism with faith, their killing with abstention, and their fornication with chastity; this indicates that it occurs in this world. Among those who held this meaning were Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. The second view is that this occurs in the Hereafter; this was said by Salman (may Allah be pleased with him), Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and 'Ali ibn al-Husayn.

'Amr ibn Maymun said: Allah replaces the evil deeds of the believer with good deeds when He forgives them for him, to the extent that the servant wishes his evil deeds had been more than they were. It is related from al-Hasan that he held both views. It is also related from al-Hasan that he said: "Some people will wish on the Day of Resurrection that they had multiplied their sins in this world." It was asked: "Who are they?" He said: "They are those about whom Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Those, Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds﴾." This view is confirmed by the hadith of Abu Dharr from the Prophet (ﷺ): "A man will be brought forth on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: 'Present to him his minor sins,' and his minor sins will be presented to him, and his major sins will be kept away from him. It will be said: 'You did on such and such a day such and such,' and he will acknowledge it and not deny it, while he fears the major sins. It will be said: 'Give him in place of every evil deed he did a good deed.'" Muslim narrated it in his Sahih.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: That is, from one who has not killed and has not committed adultery. ﴿And does righteous deeds﴾, for I have given them precedence and favoured them over those who fought My Prophet and made lawful My sacred prohibitions.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed he turns to Allah with a (sincere) return﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: Its meaning is: whoever intends repentance and aims at its reality, it is fitting for him to intend Allah by it and not mix with it what corrupts it. This is like when a man says: "Whoever trades, he trades in cloth, and whoever debates, he debates in grammar," meaning: whoever intends that, it is fitting for him to aim at this craft. He said: It is also possible that the meaning of [this] verse is: whoever repents and does righteous deeds, then his reward and recompense will be magnified for him with his Lord, to whom he directed his repentance. Since His saying: ﴿Then indeed he turns to Allah with a return﴾ conveys this meaning, it suffices from it. This is like when a man says to another man: "When you speak, know that (p-109) you are speaking to the vizier," meaning: you are speaking to one who knows your speech and will reward you. Similar to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If my standing (before you) and my reminding you of the signs of Allah is burdensome to you, then upon Allah I have relied﴾ [Yunus: 71], meaning: indeed I rely upon the One who helps me and does not forsake me. Some people said: The meaning of the verse is: indeed he returns to Allah with a return by which He accepts it from him.

The first: sins, said by al-Hasan. The second: the harm the polytheists inflicted upon them, said by Mujahid. The third: falsehood, said by Qatada. The fourth: shirk, said by al-Dahhak. Others among the people of language said: they do not remain in their former state as if they had not heard and had not seen, even though they did not literally fall down. And what is more comforting to the eye of the believer than to see his wife and children obeying Allah? By Allah, the people sought nothing but that Allah be obeyed, so that their eyes be comforted. Al-Farra' said: He said "qurrah" because it is of the form "fuʿl," and the form "fuʿl" is hardly pluralized; do you not see His saying: ﴿And call for destruction many times﴾ [al-Furqan: 14], where He did not pluralize it? And "qurrah" is a verbal noun; one says: "qarrat ʿaynuhu qurrah" (his eye was comforted, a comfort); and if it were said "qurrat ʿayn" or "qirat a'yun," it would be correct. Others said: the root of "qurrah" is from coolness, because the Arabs are harmed by heat and find relief in coolness.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And make us a leader for the righteous﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions.

One: make us leaders who are followed, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Others said: this is from the singular used to mean the plural, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 16], and His saying: ﴿For indeed they are an enemy to me﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 77].

The second: make us those who follow the righteous and take them as examples, said by Mujahid; according to this, the expression is inverted (maqlub), and the meaning is: and make the righteous a leader for us.

Others said: al-Ghurfah (the chamber) is every lofty, elevated building, and what is meant is the chambers of Paradise, which are made of chrysolite, pearls and rubies. ﴿For what they endured with patience﴾ in their religion and in the harm inflicted by the polytheists.

Ibn 'Abbas said: some of them greet one another with peace, and the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, sends peace to them. Muqatil said: "taḥiyyah" means greeting, and "salaman" means that Allah has made their affair secure for them and has overlooked them.

This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

"Whoever wills may lower himself into a narrow, deep pit,
but who has (the means) to get out of the narrow place?"

That is: to get out of the narrow place. Is this address to the believers or to the disbelievers? There are two opinions on this.
